claim: Chronic pain is associated with hypersensitivity at the site of tissue injury.
source: It is notably associated with hypersensitivity at the site of tissue injury.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract without specific data from this study, drawing on general scientific knowledge.

claim: Chronic pain in one limb in rats increased the aversive response to acute pain stimuli in the opposite limb.
source: Here, we showed that chronic pain in one limb in rats increased the aversive response to acute pain stimuli in the opposite limb, as assessed by conditioned place aversion.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by behavioral experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Neural activities in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) correlated with noxious intensities.
source: Interestingly, neural activities in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) correlated with noxious intensities
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings and decoding analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Optogenetic modulation of ACC neurons showed bidirectional control of the aversive response to acute pain.
source: optogenetic modulation of ACC neurons showed bidirectional control of the aversive response to acute pain.
evidence: This is demonstrated by optogenetic activation (Figure 3) and inhibition (Figure 4) experiments.

claim: Chronic pain altered acute pain intensity representation in the ACC to increase the aversive response to noxious stimuli at anatomically unrelated sites.
source: Chronic pain, however, altered acute pain intensity representation in the ACC to increase the aversive response to noxious stimuli at anatomically unrelated sites.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in CFA-treated rats showing altered neural tuning curves and decoding accuracy (Figure 2G-L).

claim: Chronic pain can disrupt cortical circuitry to enhance the aversive experience in a generalized anatomically nonspecific manner.
source: Thus, chronic pain can disrupt cortical circuitry to enhance the aversive experience in a generalized anatomically nonspecific manner.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined behavioral, electrophysiological, and optogenetic data.

claim: The mechanisms for sensory and affective hypersensitivity at the site of chronic pain have been well investigated.
source: The mechanisms for such sensory and affective hypersensitivity at the site of chronic pain have been well investigated.
evidence: This statement refers to existing literature without providing specific citations in this sentence.

claim: Conditions such as fibromyalgia and persistent postoperative pain raise the possibility that chronic pain may increase the aversive reaction towards noxious stimuli in an anatomically nonspecific distribution.
source: However, conditions such as fibromyalgia and persistent postoperative pain raise the possibility that chronic pain may also increase the aversive reaction towards noxious stimuli in an anatomically nonspecific distribution (Scudds et al., 1987; Petzke et al., 2003; Kehlet et al., 2006; Kudel et al., 2007; Scott et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous clinical studies.

claim: The anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) has a crucial role in the affective-aversive experience of pain.
source: The anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) has a crucial role in the affective-aversive experience of pain (Lubar, 1964; Foltz and White, 1968; Turnbull, 1972; Talbot et al., 1995; Craig et al., 1996; Rainville et al., 1997; Koyama et al., 2000; Johansen et al., 2001; Koyama et al., 2001; LaGraize et al., 2006; Qu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The ACC receives nociceptive inputs from the medial thalamus as well as from other cortical regions.
source: The ACC receives nociceptive inputs from the medial thalamus as well as from other cortical regions (Vogt and Sikes, 2000; Shyu et al., 2010).
evidence: This anatomical claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Individual ACC neurons can respond to noxious stimuli by increasing firing rates.
source: Individual ACC neurons can respond to noxious stimuli by increasing firing rates (Sikes and Vogt, 1992; Yamamura et al., 1996; Hutchison et al., 1999; Kung et al., 2003; Iwata et al., 2005; Kuo and Yen, 2005; Zhang et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous electrophysiological studies and confirmed by data in this study (Figure 2C).

claim: ACC neurons provide evaluation for the intensity of acute pain.
source: Individual ACC neurons can respond to noxious stimuli by increasing firing rates (Sikes and Vogt, 1992; Yamamura et al., 1996; Hutchison et al., 1999; Kung et al., 2003; Iwata et al., 2005; Kuo and Yen, 2005; Zhang et al., 2011) to provide evaluation for the intensity of acute pain (Coghill et al., 1999; Büchel et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations and confirmed by the decoding analysis in Figure 2F.

claim: The ACC is necessary and sufficient for the acquisition of stable aversive learning in the chronic pain condition.
source: While previous studies have demonstrated that the ACC is necessary and sufficient for the acquisition of stable aversive learning in the chronic pain condition (Johansen et al., 2001; Qu et al., 2011; Barthas et al., 2015; Navratilova et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Chronic pain has been shown to induce synaptic plasticity in ACC neurons, resulting in hypersensitivity at the site of injury through descending modulation.
source: Furthermore, chronic pain has been shown to induce synaptic plasticity in ACC neurons, resulting in hypersensitivity at the site of injury through descending modulation (Wu et al., 2005; Li et al., 2010; Koga et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Latency to paw withdrawal was shorter with higher intensity pain stimulus (HS) than lower intensity stimulus (LS).
source: Latency to paw withdrawal was shorter with higher intensity pain stimulus (HS) than lower intensity stimulus (LS). n = 12; p<0.0001, Student's t test.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B with statistical analysis.

claim: Rats spent less time in the chamber paired with HS during the test phase than at baseline, and more time in the chamber paired with NS.
source: During conditioning, rats received HS in one chamber and NS in the other chamber. After conditioning, rats spent less time in the chamber paired with HS during the test phase than at baseline, and more time in the chamber paired with NS. n = 14; p<0.0001, paired Student's t test.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1C with statistical analysis.

claim: Rats spent less time in the chamber paired with LS during the test phase than at baseline, and more time in the chamber paired with NS.
source: After conditioning with LS and NS in separate chambers, rats spent less time in the chamber paired with LS during the test phase than at baseline, and more time in the chamber paired with NS. n = 14; p=0.0131.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1D with statistical analysis.

claim: Rats spent less time in the chamber paired with HS during the test phase than at baseline, and more time in the chamber paired with LS.
source: After conditioning with HS and LS, rats spent less time in the chamber paired with HS during the test phase than at baseline, and more time in the chamber paired with LS. n = 10; p=0.0012.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1E with statistical analysis.

claim: 10 days after CFA treatment, rats spent less time in the chamber paired with HS stimulation of the uninjected paw than at baseline, and more time in the chamber paired with NS.
source: 10 days after CFA treatment, rats underwent conditioning by receiving HS stimulation of the uninjected paw in one chamber and NS stimulation of the same paw in the other chamber. During the test phase, rats spent less time in the chamber paired with HS than at baseline, and more time in the chamber paired with NS. n = 9; p<0.0001; paired Student's t test.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1F with statistical analysis.

claim: After CFA treatment, rats spent less time in the chamber paired with LS stimulation of the uninjected paw during the test phase than at baseline, and more time in the chamber paired with NS.
source: After CFA treatment, after conditioning with LS and NS in separate chambers, rats spent less time in the chamber paired with LS stimulation of the uninjected paw during the test phase than at baseline, and more time in the chamber paired with NS. n = 9; p=0.0002.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1G with statistical analysis.

claim: After CFA treatment, rats could not differentiate between HS and LS treatments of the uninjected paws on the CPA test.
source: After CFA treatment, rats could not differentiate between HS and LS treatments of the uninjected paws on the CPA test. n = 13; p=0.4923.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1H with statistical analysis.

claim: CFA treatment resulted in increased aversive response to LS.
source: CFA treatment resulted in increased aversive response to LS. Rats were conditioned with LS and NS, and the CPA or aversion score was calculated by subtracting the amount of time rats spent during the test phase from baseline in the LS-paired chamber (see Materials and methods section). CPA scores for CFA-treated rats were significantly higher than saline control. n = 9–10; p=0.0179, unpaired Student's t test.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1I with statistical analysis.

claim: CFA-treated rats demonstrated a significant decrease in the CPA score for HS, indicating an inability to distinguish between the aversive values of HS and LS.
source: After CFA treatment, rats could not distinguish between HS and LS. Rats were conditioned with HS in one chamber and LS in the other chamber. The CPA score for HS was calculated by subtracting the amount of time spent in the HS-paired chamber during the test phase from baseline. CFA-treated rats demonstrated a significant decrease in the CPA score, indicating an inability to distinguish between the aversive values of HS and LS. n = 8–13; p=0.0029, unpaired Student's t test.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1J with statistical analysis.

claim: CFA treatment did not alter paw withdrawal latency in the uninjected paw.
source: CFA treatment did not alter paw withdrawal latency in the uninjected paw. n = 12; p=0.8381, two-way ANOVA with repeated measures and post-hoc Bonferroni test.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1K with statistical analysis.

claim: CFA treatment caused mechanical allodynia in the injected but not uninjected paw.
source: CFA treatment caused mechanical allodynia in the injected but not uninjected paw. n = 12; p<0.0001. two-way ANOVA with repeated measures and post-hoc Bonferroni test.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1L with statistical analysis.

claim: A number of neurons in the ACC increased their firing rates after an acute pain stimulus.
source: We found that a number of neurons in the ACC increased their firing rates after an acute pain stimulus (see Materials and methods; Figure 2C), similar to reports from human studies (Hutchison et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2C and cited human studies.

claim: A significant number of neurons responded to noxious stimulation and showed increased firing rate after HS than LS.
source: We also found a significant number of neurons that responded to noxious stimulation and at the same time showed increased firing rate after HS than LS (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: Population-decoding analysis yielded high accuracy in distinguishing between NS and HS (85% accuracy) or between LS and HS (76% accuracy).
source: Our decoding analysis yielded high accuracy in distinguishing between NS and HS (85% accuracy) or between LS and HS (76% accuracy) (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by machine learning analysis of neural data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: After CFA injection in the opposite foot, neurons in the ACC continued to respond to pain stimuli.
source: After CFA injection in the opposite foot, we continued to find neurons in the ACC that responded to pain stimuli (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2H.

claim: SVM decoding algorithm continued to distinguish HS from NS (80% accuracy) and HS from LS (67% accuracy) after CFA treatment.
source: In addition, our SVM decoding algorithm continued to distinguish HS from NS (80% accuracy) and HS from LS (67% accuracy) (Figure 2J)
evidence: This is supported by machine learning analysis shown in Figure 2J.

claim: In the chronic pain condition, neurons showed a flatter tuning curve, as indicated by a significant decrease in the slope of linear fit.
source: In the chronic pain condition, however, neurons showed a flatter tuning curve, as indicated by a significant decrease in the slope of linear fit (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of neural tuning curves shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Chronic pain caused a statistically significant decrease in the ability to decode the difference between LS and HS signals (control vs. CFA: 76% vs 67% accuracy).
source: Furthermore, our unbiased machine learning analysis also indicated that chronic pain caused a statistically significant decrease in the ability to decode the difference between LS and HS signals (control vs. CFA: 76% vs 67% accuracy, Figure 2L).
evidence: This is supported by machine learning analysis shown in Figure 2L with statistical comparison.

claim: Brief ACC activation did not alter paw withdrawal latency to noxious stimuli.
source: We did not observe any changes in paw withdrawal latency with optogenetic stimulation (Figure 3C), suggesting that brief ACC activation did not strongly modulate the acute nocifensive reflex.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ACC activation during the presentation of LS increased the aversive response to LS.
source: We found that ACC activation during the presentation of LS increased the aversive response to LS, as shown by an avoidance of the chamber associated with optogenetic activation during the test phase compared with baseline (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic behavioral data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ACC activation during NS stimulation did not turn an acute non-noxious stimulus into a noxious one.
source: This pain-enhancing effect of ACC activation was not observed when the animal was presented with NS stimulation (Figure 3E), indicating that while transient ACC activation does not turn an acute non-noxious stimulus into a noxious one, it can significantly enhance the aversive quality of a noxious stimulus.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic behavioral data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: ACC activation during the presentation of HS increased the aversive response to HS, but this effect was not statistically significant.
source: Meanwhile, ACC activation during the presentation of HS increased the aversive response to HS on the CPA, but this effect was not statistically significant (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic behavioral data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The amplitude of the additional aversive effect provided by ACC activation during the presentation of LS is similar to the effect of chronic pain.
source: We found that these two CPA scores were nearly identical (Figure 3H). Thus, the amplitude of the additional aversive effect provided by ACC activation during the presentation of LS is similar to the effect of chronic pain.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of CPA scores shown in Figure 3H.

claim: ACC inhibition decreased the aversive response to LS.
source: We found that ACC inhibition decreased the aversive response to LS and HS, as shown by increased amounts of time spent in the chamber associated with LS or HS coupled with ACC inhibition during the test phase compared with baseline (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic behavioral data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ACC inhibition decreased the aversive response to HS.
source: We found that ACC inhibition decreased the aversive response to LS and HS, as shown by increased amounts of time spent in the chamber associated with LS or HS coupled with ACC inhibition during the test phase compared with baseline (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic behavioral data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: ACC inhibition coupled with LS stimulation removed the avoidance of the LS-paired chamber.
source: After conditioning, we found that ACC inhibition coupled with LS stimulation removed the avoidance of the LS-paired chamber (Figure 4E, p>0.05).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic behavioral data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: ACC inhibition during HS removed the higher aversive value of HS compared with LS, by eliminating the avoidance of HS-paired chamber.
source: Similarly, ACC inhibition during HS removed the higher aversive value of HS compared with LS, by eliminating the avoidance of HS-paired chamber (Figure 4F, p>0.05).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic behavioral data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: ACC inhibition abolished the aversive value of LS even in CFA-treated rats.
source: We have shown that CFA-treated rats demonstrated an increased aversive response to LS in the uninjected paw (Figure 1G). Here, we found that ACC inhibition during LS eliminated the avoidance of LS-paired chamber in CFA-treated rats when these rats were conditioned with NS (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic behavioral data in CFA-treated rats shown in Figure 4G.

claim: ACC inhibition during LS stimulations restored the normal aversive scale in CFA-treated rats, by reinstating the avoidance of HS chamber.
source: Furthermore, rats in chronic pain have been shown to lose the ability to differentiate between LS and HS on the CPA test (Figure 1H). ACC inhibition during LS stimulations, however, restored the normal aversive scale in CFA-treated rats, by reinstating the avoidance of HS chamber (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic behavioral data in CFA-treated rats shown in Figure 4H.

claim: ACC inhibition reduced the CPA score and hence the aversive response for LS even in rats with chronic pain.
source: We found that ACC inhibition reduced this CPA score and hence the aversive response for LS even in rats with chronic pain.
evidence: This is supported by CPA score analysis shown in Figure 4I.

claim: ACC inhibition during LS elevated the CPA score for HS and hence reinstated the difference in aversive values between HS and LS in rats with chronic pain.
source: We found that ACC inhibition during LS elevated the CPA score for HS and hence reinstated the difference in aversive values between HS and LS in rats with chronic pain.
evidence: This is supported by CPA score analysis shown in Figure 4J.

claim: ACC inhibition restored the normal aversive response to acute pain in those rats with chronic pain.
source: Thus, ACC inhibition restored the normal aversive response to acute pain in those rats with chronic pain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic inhibition experiments in CFA-treated rats (Figures 4G-J).

claim: Neural activities in the ACC play a vital role in the generalized enhancement of aversion in chronic pain conditions.
source: These results strongly indicate that neural activities in the ACC play a vital role in the generalized enhancement of aversion in chronic pain conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined optogenetic and behavioral experiments.

claim: Epidemiological studies have shown that the presence of chronic pain coincides with increased pain severity and a similar distortion of pain intensity scale in a diffuse anatomic pattern.
source: Epidemiological studies have shown that the presence of chronic pain coincides with increased pain severity and a similar distortion of pain intensity scale in a diffuse anatomic pattern (Scudds et al., 1987; Petzke et al., 2003; Kehlet et al., 2006; Kudel et al., 2007; Scott et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: This study provides a causal link between chronic pain and a generalized enhancement of pain aversion.
source: Our study confirms these clinical findings by providing a causal link between chronic pain and a generalized enhancement of pain aversion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: Chronic pain can induce maladaptive synaptic plasticity in the ACC.
source: Previous studies have found that chronic pain can induce maladaptive synaptic plasticity in the ACC (Li et al., 2010; Koga et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ACC neurons project to or receive inputs from a number of regions important for pain processing, including the prefrontal cortex, medial thalamus, insular cortex, amygdala, nucleus accumbens, hippocampus.
source: At the network level, ACC neurons are known to project to or receive inputs from a number of regions important for pain processing, including the prefrontal cortex, medial thalamus, insular cortex, amygdala, nucleus accumbens, hippocampus, etc.
evidence: This is stated as established anatomical knowledge without specific citations in this sentence.

claim: Acute pain likely triggers a concerted neural response in an interconnected network as suggested by fMRI studies.
source: Thus, acute pain likely triggers a concerted neural response in an interconnected network as suggested by fMRI studies (Schweinhardt and Bushnell, 2012; Wager et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to fMRI studies.

claim: The rostral region of the ACC is required specifically for the acquisition of stable aversive learning induced by chronic pain.
source: Prior lesion and pharmacological studies have shown that the rostral region of the ACC is required specifically for the acquisition of stable aversive learning induced by chronic pain (Johansen et al., 2001; Johansen and Fields, 2004; Qu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous lesion and pharmacological studies.

claim: The ACC is necessary and sufficient for the temporal regulation of the aversive response to acute pain stimuli.
source: Our study indicates that this brain region is also necessary and sufficient for the temporal regulation of the aversive response to acute pain stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic experiments in this study.

claim: Brief activation of the ACC did not cause an aversive reaction to a non-noxious stimulus.
source: Interestingly, in our study, brief activation of the ACC did not cause an aversive reaction to a non-noxious stimulus, whereas previous studies demonstrate that repeated activation of ACC neurons itself can be an aversive teaching signal (Johansen and Fields, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by the optogenetic data in Figure 3E and contrasted with cited previous studies.

claim: Repeated and possibly prolonged activation of ACC is required for the acquisition of stable aversive memory, whereas transient activation provides context-specific aversive valuation and response.
source: This difference suggests that repeated and possibly prolonged activation of ACC is required for the acquisition of stable aversive memory, whereas transient activation provides context-specific aversive valuation and response.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the comparison of current findings with previous studies.

claim: Persistent peripheral nociceptive inputs have been shown to trigger opioid signaling and synaptic plasticity in the ACC to regulate sensory and aversive components of chronic pain.
source: At the molecular and cellular level, persistent peripheral nociceptive inputs have been shown to trigger opioid signaling and synaptic plasticity in the ACC to regulate sensory and aversive components of chronic pain (Li et al., 2010; Navratilova et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The anterior cingulate cortex is involved in a number of sensory, affective and cognitive processes.
source: In addition to pain regulation, the anterior cingulate cortex is also involved in a number of sensory, affective and cognitive processes (de Araujo et al., 2003; Rolls et al., 2003; Grabenhorst et al., 2008; Rolls et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The ACC plays an important role in reward-based learning, such as providing necessary evaluation for rewarding or aversive cues as well as for the interpretation of errors in predicting such cues.
source: It plays an important role in reward-based learning, such as providing necessary evaluation for rewarding or aversive cues as well as for the interpretation of errors in predicting such cues (Bush et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The ACC plays roles in attention and in conflict monitoring.
source: It also plays roles in attention and in conflict monitoring (Braver et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Given the complexity and diversity of ACC functions and anatomic connections, plasticity within the ACC as the result of chronic pain can alter the regulation of general aversive responses.
source: However, given the complexity and diversity of its functions and anatomic connections, it is perhaps not surprising that plasticity within the ACC as the result of chronic pain can alter the regulation of general aversive responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the known functions of the ACC and the findings of this study.

claim: The ACC is likely to be an important node in a complex network of brain structures that regulate this generalized enhancement in pain aversion.
source: It should be noted, in addition, that given its rich functional connectivity, the ACC is likely to be an important node in a complex network of brain structures that regulate this generalized enhancement in pain aversion.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the known connectivity of the ACC.

claim: This mechanism of generalized enhancement of pain aversion may underpin the pathophysiology of diffuse pain syndromes such as fibromyalgia and chronic postoperative pain.
source: This mechanism of generalized enhancement of pain aversion may underpin the pathophysiology of diffuse pain syndromes such as fibromyalgia and chronic postoperative pain.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about the clinical implications of the findings.

claim: Other conditions such as depression and anxiety may exert similar impact on acute pain or other sensory and affective processes in general.
source: It also raises the possibility that other conditions such as depression and anxiety may exert similar impact on acute pain or other sensory and affective processes in general.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential broader implications.

claim: Higher laser output transferred more heat to induce more intense thermal pain.
source: The intensity of the stimulus corresponded to the power output of the laser. Higher laser output transferred more heat to induce more intense thermal pain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by temperature measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: NS did not typically elicit withdrawals within 5 s of stimulation (<5%).
source: At the behavioral level, NS did not typically elicit withdrawals within 5 s of stimulation (<5%), whereas HS and LS both elicited paw withdrawals 100% of the time.
evidence: This is a behavioral observation from the experiments.

claim: HS and LS both elicited paw withdrawals 100% of the time.
source: At the behavioral level, NS did not typically elicit withdrawals within 5 s of stimulation (<5%), whereas HS and LS both elicited paw withdrawals 100% of the time.
evidence: This is a behavioral observation from the experiments.

claim: HS elicited withdrawals with a shorter latency than LS.
source: In addition, HS elicited withdrawals with a shorter latency than LS (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Rats can detect not only the presence of acute pain, but also the aversive values of higher vs lower-intensity noxious stimuli.
source: Together, these results indicate that rats can detect not only the presence of acute pain, but also the aversive values of higher vs lower-intensity noxious stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the CPA experiments shown in Figures 1C-E.

claim: This quantitative distinction in aversive response correlates well with changes in nocifensive spinal reflex.
source: This quantitative distinction in aversive response correlates well with changes in nocifensive spinal reflex (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing the CPA results with withdrawal latency data.

claim: The effect of chronic pain on acute pain responses at anatomically unrelated sites is likely specific for the aversive component, sparing the sensory component.
source: Thus, the effect of chronic pain on acute pain responses at anatomically unrelated sites is likely specific for the aversive component, sparing the sensory component.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that CFA did not alter withdrawal latency or mechanical sensitivity in the uninjected paw (Figures 1K, 1L).

claim: Unilateral noxious stimulations can in some cases cause bilateral changes in spinal circuits regulating mechanical sensitivity.
source: There have been reports suggesting that unilateral noxious stimulations can in some cases cause bilateral changes in spinal circuits regulating mechanical sensitivity (Gao and Ji, 2010, Gao et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The identification of neurons that responded to noxious intensity is compatible with previous reports.
source: The identification of such neurons that responded to noxious intensity is also compatible with previous reports (Sikes and Vogt, 1992; Yamamura et al., 1996; Hutchison et al., 1999; Kung et al., 2003; Iwata et al., 2005; Kuo and Yen, 2005; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous electrophysiological studies.

claim: There was no significant difference in the gross motor responses to LS and HS.
source: These results indicate that there was no significant difference in the gross motor responses to LS and HS, in contrast to the dramatic difference in neural responses in the ACC seen in Figure 2.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of withdrawal velocity shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The neural responses observed in the ACC were less likely to be related to stimulus-induced movement.
source: Thus, the neural responses we observed were less likely to be related to stimulus-induced movement.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the lack of difference in motor responses between LS and HS.

claim: Neural responses in the ACC more likely represented nociceptive processing.
source: Such responses in the ACC more likely represented nociceptive processing, compatible with previous reports (Sikes and Vogt, 1992; Hutchison et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2003; Kuo and Yen, 2005; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: This impaired distinction between LS and HS by ACC neurons correlates very well with behavioral findings that showed increases in the aversive valuation of LS in the chronic pain state.
source: This impaired distinction between LS and HS by ACC neurons correlates very well with behavioral findings that showed increases in the aversive valuation of LS in the chronic pain state (Figure 1G–J), suggesting that the ACC likely plays a role in the impact of chronic pain on the acute pain experience.
evidence: This is a correlation drawn between neural and behavioral findings.

claim: 95.8 ± 1.4% of the YFP-positive cells were also VGLUTs-positive, suggesting that ChR2 was expressed almost exclusively in excitatory neurons.
source: The extent of YFP-ChR2 expression in excitatory neurons was calculated, and 95.8 ± 1.4% of the YFP-positive cells were also VGLUTs-positive, suggesting that ChR2 was expressed almost exclusively in excitatory neurons. n = 8 sections from three rats.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 92.0 ± 3.1% of the YFP-positive neurons were also VGLUTs-positive, suggesting that NpHR was expressed almost exclusively in excitatory neurons.
source: The extent of YFP-NpHR expression in excitatory neurons was calculated, and 92.0 ± 3.1% of the YFP-positive neurons were also VGLUTs-positive, suggesting that NpHR was expressed almost exclusively in excitatory neurons. n = 7 sections from three rats.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Light activation of the ACC did not change locomotor activities during the test.
source: We measured locomotion over 10 min for rats that received optogenetic activation of the ACC. Light was turned on for 3 s every 10 s during the locomotion test. Light treatment did not change locomotor activities during the test. n = 8; p=0.6517, paired Student's t test.
evidence: This is supported by locomotion test data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Light inhibition of the ACC did not impact free movements of the animals.
source: Inhibition of the ACC did not impact free movements of the animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by locomotion test data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Shining light in the ACC injected with a YFP-only vector without opsin expression did not result in any changes in pain aversion phenotypes.
source: Furthermore, as expected, shining light in the ACC injected with a YFP-only vector without opsin expression did not result in any changes in pain aversion phenotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a control experiment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: ACC inhibition had no effect on the aversive response to NS.
source: Furthermore, as expected, ACC inhibition had no effect on the aversive response to NS, which was not noxious (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic behavioral data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: There was not a statistically significant difference in the average velocity of withdrawal between the responses to LS and HS.
source: There was not a statistically significant difference in the average velocity of withdrawal between the responses to LS and HS. n = 7 rats for each stimulus. p=0.4503, unpaired Student's t test.
evidence: This is supported by paw withdrawal velocity measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Averaged temperature at the time of recordings was 40.2 ± 1.9, 53.1 ± 2.1, and 61.4 ± 1.6 for NS, LS and HS, respectively.
source: Averaged temperature at the time of recordings was 40.2 ± 1.9, 53.1 ± 2.1, and 61.4 ± 1.6 for NS, LS and HS, respectively. p=0.0003 for comparison between NS and LS, <0.0001 for comparison between NS and HS, and 0.0123 for comparison between LS and HS. n = 10–24 recording sessions.
evidence: This is supported by temperature measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: SVM analysis using a shorter 3 s time window to distinguish between HS and NS (83%) or HS and LS (76%) yielded similar results to analysis using a longer 5 s time window.
source: SVM analysis using a shorter 3 s time window to distinguish between HS and NS (83%) or HS and LS (76%) yielded similar results to analysis using a longer 5 s time window (Figure 2F). n = 9.
evidence: This is supported by additional decoding analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The maximum decoding accuracy for distinguishing NS from HS was 0.83.
source: Time zero denotes the laser onset. The blue curve denotes the decoding accuracy (n1 = 24 trials for NS, n2 = 32 trials for HS; C = 7 ACC neurons) derived from the data with true labels; the error bar denotes the SEM from 100 Monte Carlo simulations based on 5-fold cross-validation; the maximum decoding accuracy was 0.83.
evidence: This is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The chance level decoding accuracy was 53%.
source: The red curve denotes the decoding accuracy derived from the shuffled data with randomly permuted labels; the error bar denotes the SEM from 500 random permutations; the maximum decoding accuracy was 0.53. The chance level 53% (instead of 50%) was partially due to the imbalance of the sample size (n1≠ n2).
evidence: This is supported by shuffled data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.
